subject: correct mirt.model statement for bifactor model with correlated factor?

messages.author: c1c3dbde7a2d806d
messages.subject: correct mirt.model statement for bifactor model with correlated factor?
parts:
Hi,

I tried to fit a bifactor model with one general and a couple of domain factors and a correlated factor. An example for the Q-matrix specification:

#Loadings as Q-Matrix

Q <- matrix(

cbind(

c(rep(1, times=30), rep(0, times=10)),

c(rep(1, times=10), rep(0, times=30)),

c(rep(0, times=10), rep(1, times=10), rep(0, times=20)),

c(rep(0, times=20), rep(1, times=10), rep(0, times=10)),

c(rep(0, times=30), rep(1, times=10))

), ncol=5, dimnames = list(NULL, c('General', 'Dim1', 'Dim2', 'Dim3', 'AddFact'))

)

Q

#And as covariances -- sixth factor (AddFact) correlated with all other factors

#and the Covariance Matrix

cov.factors <- matrix(FALSE, ncol=5, nrow=5)

diag(cov.factors) <- TRUE

cov.factors[,5] <- TRUE

cov.factors[5,] <- TRUE

cov.factors

#I used T/F as in the manual; 0/1 does not work either

The problem is: when running this then with mirt, the Covariance-Matrix from the model is estimated as a diagonal matrix, no correlations between the additional factor and the other factors are estimated.

Where did I go wrong?
And sorry in advance, if it is a stupid blunder on my side!
jan

messages.author: b330c2028fed415b
messages.subject: Re: correct mirt.model statement for bifactor model with correlated factor?
parts:
Hi Jan,

Using the above definitions, pass the objects to mirt.model(), where 

model <- mirt.model(Q, COV=cov.factors)

and further send this on to mirt(). Unfortunately, on the current versions the variance terms are not freely estimated this way (only the covariances), but on the dev version variances are now detected. Either way, freeing variance terms is generally risky buisness since the models will become unidentified quickly, so I'd recommend leaving them as fixed at 1 for now. 

Also, this isn't strictly a bifactor model (see ?bfactor for details), so you won't be able to capitalize on dimension reduction techniques for working with a larger number of latent variables. Given 5 factors, your best bet is probably the MHRM algorithm. Hope that helps.

Phil
